News.title: My son was a sweet teddy bear who turned into a demon, I drove him to the woods to shoot him, I only wish he had died
News.content:
MONSTER'S MOTHER My son was a sweet teddy bear who turned into a demon, I drove him to the woods to shoot him, I only wish he had died

WHEN he was a young child, Jeanette Halton-Tiggs adored her son, Timmy, who had chubby cheeks and liked to wear a suit and tie like the ministers in church.

“He wanted to be a minister and told me, ‘Mama, I have to look the part,’” says Jeanette.





It’s a memory that makes her smile – but that is soon eclipsed by the darkest of shadows, that saw her son grow up with a love for inflicting pain on his younger sister, escalating into violent outbursts on others and the shooting of a police officer.

Terrified for the safety of her family, Jeanette made the unthinkable decision to kill her own son. She drove to the park to shoot him and aimed her gun at him but couldn’t go through with it at the last moment.

“Timmy was my big sweet teddy bear that morphed into a monster,” she says. “I love my son dearly, but if I would have killed him, police officer Jason West would still be alive.”

In the TV documentary, Evil Lives Here: My Child The Killer, Jeanette talks about her fears and the trauma of watching her cherubic son turn into a demon.

“As a parent, you always blame yourself. You always question, ‘Did I do enough? What could I have done different? I mean, he was just so adorable growing up, with those cheeks that everybody would squeeze. I have a lot of happy memories. I just have a lot of sad ones, too.”



A year after Timmy was born, Jeanette gave birth to her daughter, Chrissy. The following year, she filed for divorce.

“Married at 16, two kids by 17, divorced at 18. I didn’t know how to do this thing. I didn’t know how to raise children. They were being raised along with me.”



Her grandmother helped watch the children while Jeanette worked two jobs in her home town of Cleveland, Ohio.

“It was hard. My son would be on the sidewalk, looking down the street at his father, who didn’t visit him, teaching another kid how to ride a bike.

“He was influenced by seeing his grandfather preaching from the church pulpit and his father playing the organ and wanted to go to bible school to study to become a minister.

“He wanted to ‘look the part’ from an early age so we would go to the department store and while I’m looking for T-shirts, sweatshirts and pants, he’d be off in the little suit department and I couldn’t say no to him. He’d be so happy. He was like a little man. He thought he was man of the house and was my protector.

“He was so loving and he and his sister were so close. They were best friends. But then he changed.



“One day I smelt something really foul and I’m looking around and finally, I checked under Timmy’s bed and opened a shoe box to find a dead bird inside that had been cut open. It freaked me out.

“I called him in and I asked him about it and he didn’t answer at first but then he said, ‘I was just putting it out of its misery.’

“I did not want to think that my son could be cruel. I was frightened. I just knew something was wrong with him because I had heard that psychopaths start off by killing animals and I thought, maybe he is a demon.

“I made every excuse up you can. That’s what mothers do. We love our babies so much and we want the best for them. We don’t want to think the worst, but I didn’t know what was coming next.”

One night, while she was getting Chrissy ready for her bath, Jeanette noticed marks on her daughter’s leg.



“I asked her what caused them and she tried to cover them up but then said, ‘Timmy made this shocking toy and he shocks me. He burns me and he told me that if I told you he was going to get me.’

PICS

“He would tie her to a chair and, I don’t know quite how he did it, but he would take wires out of a radio and he would shock her with them. Everything became very real in that moment. He was physically abusing his little sister.

“I didn’t want to spank my children, but there was no stopping me. But even when I did that, he showed no emotion.”

Timmy promised never to hurt his sister again. But it was a promise he wouldn’t keep.



“A couple of weeks later, I came home early from work and Chrissy’s in a chair. I said, ‘Is he shocking you again?’ And she said, ‘Yeah, mummy.’

“She told me the louder she yelled or screeched, the more he laughed about it. I tried to talk to him in an attempt to get to the bottom of why he liked to inflict pain but he would just say, ‘I don’t know why.’

“The family said that we should pray the demon inside him, away. They literally wanted to do an exorcism in the church. I know there’s a God and I believe there’s hell, too. There was something evil inside of him.”

After a series of violent incidents when he was a teenager, Timmy was sent to a school for children with behavioural issues. Here, he had to be restrained in a straitjacket after attacking a teacher for asking about his father.

Despite the violence, Timmy was academically smart and was proud to be able to tell his mum he had won a place at college.



“I was so proud of him and he was so happy that I was proud of him because he had caused me so much heartache and pain. It gave me so much hope. I thought he was getting it together and that we had turned a corner.”

Unfortunately, Timmy couldn’t stop the violence inside of him. He assaulted multiple people in various incidents. “He would hang out at the mall and punch people in the head for no reason,” she said.

On 9 July, 2000, when he was 20, police got a call from Chrissy who had locked her brother out of the house. She described him as bipolar and “Violent when not properly medicated.” A disorderly conduct charge was later dismissed.

“That was part of the problem,” says Jeanette. “No matter what he did, no matter who he hurt, they dismissed him. He just got one slap on the wrist after another.”

Because of his behavioural issues, his school determined he was not ready for college. Hoping to help her son, Jeanette sent him to a psychiatric facility for evaluation. While here, he had to be put into a straitjacket again after attacking the nurses.



“I went to see him and I will never forget his face. It was not my son, I swear to God. It’s so hard to make anyone believe, but I was looking at a devil.”

After Timmy was released from the facility, his violent behaviour continued to spiral out of control.

“He would walk around the house screaming and punching holes in the walls. Chrissy was terrified of him. She had a new baby and she was scared to sleep alone so she and the baby would sleep with me. She said that if we kicked him out, he would get us. The situation was so hopeless. I bought a gun for our protection.”

One night, Chrissy called her mum in a state of terror. Timmy was on a rampage.

“I rushed home and when I got there, I saw blood on the wall and I got my gun out of my purse and looked around. I didn’t know if he was still in the house.”



Jeanette found Chrissy and her baby hiding in the closet. She had already rung the police and when they arrived, they searched the house but Timmy was not there. However, outside, they found the cat, cut up, which is where the blood came from.

In 2003, Timmy was arrested for attacking a police officer. He was put on probation for four years and had to stay medicated and monitored. It seemed to work.

“It was a miracle. I noticed a big difference. He worked six days a week. He was so proud of himself. He bought a brand new car, he finally moved out of my house and had a girlfriend. But after a year they took him off probation because he was doing so well. I said to the probation officer, ‘But what about his medication?’ and she said, ‘Oh, that ends too.’

“I was like, ‘Are you serious? Look over his records. Please reconsider. You’re going to keep letting my son go until he kills somebody.’”

Feeling like she was not getting any help from elsewhere, Jeanette decided to take matters into her own hands.



She persuaded Timmy to go to the park with her, where they sometimes used to sit on a bench. But this time she had an ulterior motive. She had packed her gun and intended to shoot him.

“I said to him, ‘Timmy, look over there,’ and he got up to look at where I was pointing and I took out my gun and pointed it at him to shoot him in the back of the head. But my hands were trembling and I just dropped it, fell to my knees, and I let out this horrible scream.

“He ran back, saying, ‘Mummy, what’s wrong?’ He didn’t understand why I was crying and I never told him.”

On 25 May, 2007, Timmy, now 27, made her worst nightmare become a reality when he shot police officer Jason West as he attended a fight in the street. In court, Timmy raged that the officer pulled a gun on him and denied shooting him but then admitted that he shot Jason, who had not drawn his gun, four times.

On 30 October, 2009, he was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole.



“After the incident, I was fearful of retaliation for my whole family,” says Jeanette. “I would be so ashamed. I would walk with my head down, hoping they didn’t recognise me. He’s the monster and I’m the monster’s mother. It’s an awful feeling.

“There’s a memorial sign to Jason West that I drive past twice a day, to work and back. I say a quick prayer for him and his family each time.

“Timmy just turned 46 but he’s still my baby. You never stop loving them. But, as awful as it sounds, I wish Timmy had died that night instead of Jason.

“That would have been a better outcome for everybody. And if I had killed him then Jason West would still be alive. I’m not proud to say that, but it’s the truth. “

Evil Lives Here: My Child The Killer, Quest Red, Thursday 30 April, 9pm

News.title: Man and woman in their 20s found dead in Premier Inn hotel room as cops probe ‘unexplained’ death
News.content:
HOTEL TRAGEDY Man and woman in their 20s found dead in Premier Inn hotel room as cops probe ‘unexplained’ death

AN INVESTIGATION has been launched after a man and a woman in their 20s were tragically found dead in a Premier Inn.

Cops launched a probe after the bodies of the pair were found in one of the rooms at the hotel in Ipswich, Suffolk, on Tuesday afternoon.



Emergency crews were scrambled to the hotel – which has 85 rooms across six floors – at around 2.30pm.

Five police cars, two police vans and an ambulance could be seen outside.



Suffolk Police confirmed the deaths are being treated as unexplained, but believe there are no suspicious circumstances.

The force said: “Police were called to an address in Key Street, Ipswich by the ambulance service shortly before 2.30pm on Tuesday.

“A man and woman were found dead within the address and their families have been notified.

“Enquiries are at an early stage and at present the deaths are being treated as unexplained, however they are currently not believed to be suspicious.”

The hotel remained open for business today.

The Sun has approached Premier Inn for comment.

News.title: Mother-in-law of ‘murdered’ beauty queen, 27, arrested after going on the run as husband ‘breastfed baby from her body’
News.content:
THE mother-in-law of murdered Mexican beauty queen Carolina Flores Gomez has been arrested after going on the run.

It comes after reports the tragic model’s husband tried to breastfeed their baby with her dead body before alerting police.





Erika Maria Herrera, 63, also known as “N” was cuffed following a major police manhunt – after 27-year-old Carolina was shot dead on April 15.

The mum-in-law and main suspect in the case was arrested in Venezuela following an urgent search.

The shooting took place at a luxury apartment in Mexico City – with horror footage showing the moments before Carolina’s death.

Carolina’s husband Alejandro said he tried to breastfeed their baby using her corpse and only alerted authorities the day after her death.



The beauty queen’s mum has accused Alejandro of deliberately delaying his call to police in order to give his own mother time to escape.

Investigators have not confirmed the claims.



Mexico police said: “The Attorney General’s Office of Mexico City confirms that, in coordination with authorities of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, Erika Maria ‘N’ was arrested as the probable person responsible for the femicide of a 27-year-old woman committed in the Miguel Hidalgo borough.

“Following the murder, the City of Mexico Prosecutor’s Office initiated an investigation that made it possible to establish her probable involvement.

“Based on the evidence gathered on April 17, one day after the complaint was filed, a judge issued the corresponding arrest warrant.”



Mexican cops were helped by Interpol and the suspect is currently being held in Venezuela pending extradition.

Carolina, a former Miss Teen Universe, was shot dead in the face, neck and head.

Her husband Alejandro has claimed he decided to stay at home and not immediately report the shooting because he wanted to feed their baby, according to local crime reporter Carlos Jimenez.



He said he tried to breastfeed the tot – as Carolina had been doing at the time – and then bathed it before calling his lawyers.

Alejandro also claimed he feared the baby could be taken into care by social services.

Chilling footage from the day of Carolina’s death shows two women walking into a room before gunshots and screaming are heard.

Herrera was inside the home with her son – Carolina’s partner – at the time of the shooting in Polanco, Mexico City.

Alejandro has not been arrested but is understood to be under investigation for failing to report his wife’s death immediately.



In the harrowing video of Carolina’s death, the former pageant winner from Baja California can be seen walking to the back of her home wearing a white robe.

Several local outlets have reported Carolina was going to get her mother-in-law a drink of water at the time.

Herrera is then seen following her before several gunshots ring out.

The victim’s husband, Alejandro, walks into the frame just seconds later, carrying the couple’s baby.

“What was that?” he asks his mother in Spanish.



“What did you do, crazy?” an unidentified person’s voice is heard saying.

“Nothing,” his mum answers. “She made me angry.”

“What’s wrong with you? She’s my family,” Alejandro says, calmly.

His mum replies: “You’re mine and she stole you”.

Spanish media outlet Debate spoke to a close friend of Carolina, who said the victim had been hounded by her mother-in-law when she fell pregnant.



The friend said Carolina believed that Herrera “never liked her” and that she had “gotten worse” since the pregnancy.

It has also been suggested that a multimillion-pound inheritance could be behind the killing.

Carolina is believed to have received a large sum of money following the death of her father.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The high-profile killing left the Mexican community reeling, sparking a wave of protests in Mexico‘s Baja California over the weekend.

Carolina was born in San Diego, was crowned Miss Teen Universe for Baja California in 2017, and picked up several local titles in her home city of Ensenada.

News.title: Beautiful £900,000 cottage holds secret so chilling its new owner is SUING seller for not revealing it
News.content:
SICK SECRET Beautiful £900,000 cottage holds secret so chilling its new owner is SUING seller for not revealing it

THE owners of a stunning cottage in Canada are suing the former owner for failing to disclose a harrowing secret about its dark past.

The buyers claim the previous owner failed to inform them that a violent killing had taken place at the picturesque home just six years earlier.





Court documents reveal that in 2018, a man named Normand James, 52, died after breaking into the property.

The schizophrenic was stabbed multiple times by the homeowner in what was later ruled self-defence.

At the time of the incident, the cottage – located in the quiet town of Hudson – was occupied by a woman in her 40s and her three children.

Police questioned her following the altercation but ultimately released her without charges.



A coroner later determined that James had attempted to flee the scene before collapsing outside the home.

He was transported to hospital, where he was pronounced dead.



Fast-forward to April 2024, when the cottage was sold to new owners who say they had no knowledge of the property’s violent history.

They now allege that this crucial omission would have significantly impacted their purchase decision, as well as the price they were willing to pay.

According to a lawsuit seen by CTV News, the buyers are now seeking £315,000 in damages in a lawsuit.

They argue that the former owners failed to properly disclose the incident in the mandatory seller’s declaration.

“If the plaintiffs been informed of this violent death … and the tragic, circumstances of this widely publicized tragedy in a timely manner, they would not have purchased the property or paid the asking price,” the lawsuit says.



Broker Mark-Andre Martel – who is not involved in the case – noted that homes tied to violent events often see a drop of 10 to 15 percent in value.

“Ultimately, when you have that type of disclosure it diminishes the pool of buyers for any given property,” Martel said.

“And if you have less buyers, well then the price will be lower as well.”

The current owners are now hoping to recoup roughly a quarter of what they paid for the home, along with additional damages.

They have also filed a separate claim against the property’s listing agent, seeking £18,000.



However, the sellers and their agent strongly dispute the allegations.

In a statement, the agent insisted that the seller’s declaration accurately reflected the known facts of the incident.

“The seller’s declaration … accurately described the incident … it would have been incorrect to indicate in that declaration that [the intruder’s] death occurred on the property, as no evidence supports such a conclusion,” she wrote.

Documents show the sellers did acknowledge an “intrusion/altercation” on the disclosure form which they maintain should have prompted further questions from the buyers if they had concerns.

Notably, the sellers answered “no” to a specific question about whether a violent death or suicide had occurred inside the property.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

James had a previous history of mental illness, and was once charged with the attempted murder of a police officer.

The woman who stabbed him faced no charge in connection with the incident.

News.title: Reform sacks councillor who called England flag a ‘crusade’ symbol in leaked messages
News.content:
Cllr Roy insisted he had 'never criticised the St George’s Cross' and said his remarks were about 'perception and perspective'

REFORM has booted out a councillor after he described England’s flag as a “crusade” symbol in leaked messages.

Cllr Aaron Roy — who had defected from Labour last month — made the remarks in a WhatsApp exchange during a row over flags in Hartlepool last year.



In the messages, he said he was “not aligned” with the use of the St George’s Cross and would “rather use a Union Jack”.



He described the issue as one of “perception vs perspective”.

Quoting a Labour message saying there was “nothing wrong” with flying flags, he asked: “Does this mean it’s ok to fly India / Palestine / Pakistan flags too??”

The St George’s Cross is England’s national flag.

Reform last week pledged to fund flagpoles for every school, requiring the Union Flag to be flown as the primary national symbol, with the St George’s Cross displayed alongside it where additional poles are available.



After The Sun approached Reform with the comments, the party moved to expel Cllr Roy.

A spokesman said last night: “Reform is proud of our nation’s flags, and there’s no place in our party for anyone with views such as those shared by Cllr Aaron Roy.

“As soon as his comments were brought to our attention he was expelled from the party.”

Cllr Roy insisted he had “never criticised the St George’s Cross” and said his remarks were about “perception and perspective”.



He said he was “proud of England and proud of Hartlepool” and added he personally preferred the Union Jack as a “unifying national symbol”.

The Indian citizen, elected as a Labour councillor in 2024, added: “The St George’s Cross has a long and well-documented historical association with the Christian Crusades, and that history is read differently by people of different backgrounds.

“My question about flags from India, Pakistan and Palestine was not a dismissal of any flag it was a test, from someone whose own family flag is one of those I named, of whether Labour’s policy was coherent, consistent and applied equally to everyone in our town.

“It is a question I was entitled to ask. It is one I would ask again.”

News.title: Secrets of wife-swapping spy who recruited Nazis to bring down Hitler – before finding fame with VERY different career
News.content:
REAL 007 Secrets of wife-swapping spy who recruited Nazis to bring down Hitler – before finding fame with VERY different career

SUAVE, well spoken and a bit of a ladies man – Peter Sichel was trusted with some of the CIA’s toughest assignments.

From recruiting former Nazi’s to bring down Adolf Hitler’s regime during World War II to running their first Berlin office during the Cold War, he was a founding father of modern espionage.





As a Jew from Germany growing up under fascism Peter understood all too well the dangers posed by despotic leaders.

He managed to escape a prison camp just before his fellow residents were sent to be exterminated.

Having been educated in Britain, Peter drew comparisons to a fictional secret agent.

The unsung hero was known as the Jewish James Bond.



Now the incredible story of Peter’s life is being told in a new documentary titled The Last Spy, where he makes revelations that surprise even his closest family members.

The once shadowy figure, who died last year aged 102, talks about helping to prevent World War III, losing brave agents behind enemy lines and the wife swapping exploits of spies.



Frustrated by the CIA repeating its mistakes, Peter left the secret service in 1960 to run the family wine business and to turn Blue Nun into one of the most famous tipples in the world.

His daughters Sylvia and Bettina both believe the twinkled-eyed spy was thrilled to be compared to 007.

Sylvia tells The Sun: “He was very charming with the ladies. Hopefully not quite as active with the ladies as James Bond.



“I think he identified with that British sensibility you guys have of a stiff upper lip or not to be too sentimental.

“I think that the way he was like James Bond is that he just acted. It’s like he would see it and then he’d do it. And there wasn’t a lot of hand wringing.”

Bettina agrees: “Yes, the ladies loved him.”

Born in Mainz in Germany in 1922, the Sichel family were well known due to their vineyards.

Peter enjoyed a private education in England, first at a prep school in Eastbourne on the south coast and then at Stowe in Buckinghamshire.



In 1934 his mother Franziska urged his dad Eugen to leave Germany fearing that “all the Jews are going to get killed” by Hitler’s thugs.

By the time his father accepted this reality it was illegal for them to leave their homeland without permission.

They managed to trick their way out, settling in Bordeaux in France.

But while Peter was visiting his family, the Nazi’s invaded and the French authorities arrested them for being “enemy aliens.”

Just a couple of days before German troops reached the camp, the Sichels escaped the internment camp and fled further south.



In the documentary Peter said: “The German Stukas strafed the refugees. When we heard them coming we jumped into the ditch.”

The men and the women were separated, with a 19-year-old Peter helping his dispirited father to find his mother and sister.

But they only had enough funds for three fake passports to get to Portugal, so Peter volunteered to attempt the journey without a forged ID.

Sylvia, 58, said: “His dad kind of fell apart when they were hiding out in France. And he had to become the man of the family.”

Bettina, 64, continues: “He elected to stay behind. And then he had to get himself across Spain. Getting himself to Portugal by himself was a daring adventure story.”



From there, they travelled to New York in the United States in 1941, where his aunt lived.

The day after the Japanese bombed Pearl Harbour, bringing the Americans into World War II, Peter volunteered for military service.

Thanks to his fluent German, he was recruited to the spy agency the Office of Strategic Services (OSS).

Peter recalled: “We were trained how to pick locks and how to kill people with a knife.”

He was dispatched to Algeria where he trained resistance fighters and aged 22 was put in charge of a vital OSS operation.



His job was to persuade German prisoners of war to join the Allies and to make sure they were genuine in their intentions.

Following D-Day, Peter led a secret service unit of a hundred men into France attached to General Patton’s 7th Army.

Peter said: “Patton lost a lot of men, if he would have listened to the intelligence it wouldn’t have happened.”

The young agent impressed the senior spooks enough to be placed in charge of the OSS’s operation in Berlin, when the city was surrounded by Communist East Germany after the end of the war.

Nicknamed the “wunderkind” he found himself getting agents out of trouble, including one who was being blackmailed by a lover.



But he couldn’t save another spy whose severed head was found by a railway track.

In 1947 the OSS became the CIA and its main mission was countering the spread of communism.

There was a fear that the Soviet Union planned to invade West Berlin, which was controlled by the US, France and Great Britain.

The Western Allies had to decide whether to counter such an attack, which could lead to World War III.

It was his job to find out if there was a significant military build up in East Germany.



Peter said: “We sent hundreds of spies on a tourist mission on bikes. They were able to find out the intentions were not aggressive. There were never any preparations to march.”

He considered that discovery to be his “greatest achievement.”

While working in Berlin he met his first wife Cuy Höttler, but he claimed she was not faithful to him.

After being relocated to Washington, the couple were drawn into boozy afternoons and late night parties.

Peter said: “We drank an enormous amount of liquor. America was awash with alcohol.”



It was the same issue when he was placed in charge of the CIA station in Hong Kong.

He recalled: “There was an active exchange of wives and everybody drank too much.”

Peter continued: “My first wife was extremely charming but had a roving eye.”

They divorced and in 1961 he wed his second wife Stella Spanoudaki, who is Sylvia and Bettina’s mum.

Gradually, Peter became disillusioned by the CIA’s attempts to “rollback” the Red peril.



Secret agents sent to both communist Ukraine and Albania during the Cold War to foment a revolution were caught and killed.

In 1959 Peter was told a similar plan was to be actioned in China, but he didn’t believe there were any resistance groups there to help them.

Rather than sending any more spies to die on a doomed mission he handed in his notice.

He explained: “I didn’t want to be responsible for the deaths of people because we don’t learn from our own experience.”

On leaving the CIA he took over from an uncle running the family’s wine business.



The Sichels made a popular Liebfraumilch with nuns on the label against the backdrop of a blue sky.

Customers would ask for the “blue nun wine” and Peter decided to market it under that name, with younger women in blue habits in the picture instead.

It was a staple of dining tables in the 1980s, with 1.25 million cases sold in the United States alone in 1984 and was even referenced in the Beastie Boys song The Blue Nun, which sampled Peter’s voice.

Peter, who also operated in Britain, was highly respected in the wine industry and Bettina, who followed him into the business, thinks that is his great legacy.

But for Sylvia, what she most admires about her dad is the way he refused to be cowed by Hitler’s reign of terror which took the lives of six million Jews.



She concludes: “His legacy is of someone who was told he wasn’t allowed to be in his country where his family had been since the 1700s and said, ‘screw that.’

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“‘I belong there and I’m going to go fight for the ideals of this country called Germany beyond this moment in history. I’m taking this back. I’m doing everything I can.’”

The Last Spy is in cinemas and on demand now.

News.title: Migrant who dragged teen into woodland and raped after avoiding deportation over his ‘human rights’ is jailed
News.content:
FREE TO ROAM Migrant who dragged teen into woodland and raped after avoiding deportation over his ‘human rights’ is jailed

A MIGRANT who dragged a teen into woodland and raped her after avoiding deportation over his “human rights” has been jailed.

Nigerian national Gift Oladele, 24, told the terrified 19-year-old “this will teach you a lesson not to trust strangers” after the attack.





The predator was already known to the authorities, having been jailed for two years in 2022 for the false imprisonment of a woman in Manchester.

Following his sentencing, the Home Office ordered his deportation but Oladele successfully appealed through the Asylum and Immigration Tribunal.

The court ruled removing him would violate Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects the right to respect for private and family life.

Once freed from jail, Oladele dragged the 19-year-old into woodland as she walked home from a night out in Wrexham, Wales.

He has now been locked up for 25 years, with 17 in custody and the rest on licence, after being convicted of rape.

Oladele, who born in Italy but a Nigerian national, arrived in the UK with entry clearance until 2014 but went on to live here illegally.



In 2022, the fiend was arrested for holding the woman captive and later told cops he “just wanted to get it on with her”.

After his conviction for the broad daylight attack, the Home Office ordered his deportation under the UK Borders Act 2007.

Oladele submitted an appeal to the Asylum and Immigration Tribunal on June 24, 2023, claiming he has a family life in the UK with his partner and that he would face insurmountable obstacles if he was sent back.

The tribunal ruled in his favour and said the refusal by the Home Office to revoke the deportation order had been a “breach of the Appellant’s protected rights” under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

A judge said: “Weighing everything, I find that the matter is finely balanced. The offence that the Appellant committed was very serious and I find that there is a strong public interest in deporting and excluding foreign criminals, especially one who has committed a frightening and public assault.



“However I have found that the factors on the Appellant’s side of the balance sheet, in particular the fact that he would be a complete outsider should he relocate to Nigeria with attendant risks, that he has a developed private life having grown up in the United Kingdom and that he has engaged positively in a process of rehabilitation and that this has had the impact of reducing the risk of reoffending, are just sufficiently compelling to outweigh those on the Respondent’s side.”

In September last year – less than three years after his conviction, Oladele put his hand over the victim’s mouth and pushed her down a path into woods.

The predator told her he would “put “a baby inside her” as he raped the woman.

She later told police: “It felt as if he had done it before. The way he did things and the way he handled me made it feel like it wasn’t the first time.”

In an emotional statement, she told the court today how she felt like she was in a “living hell” after the attack.



She said she is still not able to eat properly and was petrified he would be found not guilty.

Following Oladele’s arrest, police found evidence on his phone that showed a long standing interest in forced sexual abuse.

A Home Office spokesperson said after his conviction: “This is an absolutely horrific case, and our thoughts are with the victim of this heinous criminal.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Foreign nationals who commit crimes should be in zero doubt that we will aim to remove them from the UK at the earliest opportunity.

“The Home Secretary has announced sweeping reforms to tackle illegal migration, which will make the UK less attractive for illegal migrants and make it easier to remove them.”

News.title: Mystery of rotting £4m mansion where mummified corpse was found now swamped with 10ft knotwood jungle & swarms of bugs
News.content:
LEFT TO ROT Mystery of rotting £4m mansion where mummified corpse was found now swamped with 10ft knotwood jungle & swarms of bugs

A MYSTERIOUS rotting mansion where the mummified corpse of a man was once found has sparked fury from neighbours.

The £4million property is riddled with towering knotweed and infested with pests despite sitting on a wealthy West London street lined with luxury homes.





And now the owner has finally been ordered to clean it up after years of complaints and legal battles.

Disturbingly, a body was also found in the basement of the property back in 2010 after neighbours reported a foul smell coming from inside.

Locals have since identified the dead man only as Frank, an Irish builder who was well known in the area and had been living there as a lodger.

Residents said Frank was a regular at a nearby pub before he suddenly vanished.



When he stopped showing, neighbours became concerned.

Cops later climbed into the crumbling mansion on Ifield Road in Chelsea using a ladder from a neighbouring garden.

Inside they made the grim discovery of Frank’s decomposed body in the basement.

Neighbours claimed the corpse was so badly rotted that several officers reportedly vomited.

One young police officer who entered the property was reportedly on his very first day on the job.



Shocked residents gave the distraught copper whisky to drink in an attempt to calm him down.

More than 15 years later, the mansion has become a nightmare for people living nearby.

Locals say leaking drains have turned parts of the house into a swamp breeding mosquitoes, rats and foxes.

They claim foxes living inside the property screech through the night and keep neighbours awake.

The rear garden has also been swallowed by Japanese knotweed stretching up to 10ft high.



The invasive plant is capable of spreading into brickwork and damaging nearby homes.

Fed-up residents say the property has become a rat-infested jungle.

They also claim the shocking state of the mansion has made neighbouring properties harder to sell.

Now Kensington and Chelsea Council has stepped in and ordered owner Nicholas Halbritter to tackle the mess.

The 78-year-old has been issued with a Section 215 notice legally forcing him to clean up the property.



The action came after dozens of residents signed a petition demanding the council intervene.

At a recent council meeting, furious neighbour Nik Hoexter laid bare the scale of the problems surrounding the house.

He said: “There’s rampant knotweed, there are rats, foxes, there’s a mosquito swarm from a leaking mains, which has been going on for two years.”

He also told councillors that vegetation was growing into the house through smashed rear windows.

Summing up the state of the property, he said: “The house is rotting from the inside out.”



Neighbours have branded Mr Halbritter a “neighbour from hell” and claim he refuses to speak about the home.

Next-door resident Christine Gambles, 69, told the Daily Mail: “He beetles up the street and runs in the door.

“If I ask him for a conversation, he literally slams the door in my face.”

The mansion’s condition has shocked residents because of Mr Halbritter’s own public profile.

He is a former Conservative councillor in Kensington and Chelsea and once sat on the same committee now taking action against him.



He also serves as chairman of the borough’s branch of the Royal British Legion.

In 2022 he received an award from the borough’s mayor for his fundraising work supporting war veterans.

A year later he attended an Armed Forces reception at Downing Street.

Residents say Mr Halbritter no longer lives full-time at the Chelsea mansion but still visits regularly.

They claim his presence is often marked by a light glowing from a first-floor room.



Mr Halbritter is believed to have moved into the property with his mother Elizabeth after the death of his father Sidney.

Following Elizabeth’s death, he reportedly began renting out rooms in the home to lodgers including Frank.

Neighbours said the basement flat where the builder stayed was already in a terrible condition.

In 2016 he was served with another Section 215 notice ordering him to clear rubbish, repair windows and deal with knotweed.

After failing to comply, he later appeared before magistrates and pleaded guilty to the offence.



He was ordered to pay more than £1,500 in costs.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

A Kensington and Chelsea Council spokesperson said: “Following the decision of the Planning Applications Committee, we are proceeding with a Section 215 notice and will progress it in line with the legislation and relevant guidance.

“The 2016 notice – which was investigated by a Hammersmith & Fulham officer under a bi-borough working arrangement at the time – was considered complied with and the enforcement case was closed.”

News.title: People appalled by 1 thing American woman says she doesn't like about the UK
News.content:
People appalled by 1 thing American woman says she doesn't like about the UK

An American woman now living in Manchester with her husband and two children has said while she "loves it here", there are three things she's "not into" - and one is a very popular supermarket staple

View Image An American woman living in the UK is unimpressed with a popular feature found in the supermarket (stock image) (Image: Roy James Shakespeare/Getty Images)

An American woman living in the UK has revealed three British things she’s just “not into” and while people agreed with two features on her list, the third left many outraged. Despite both nations speaking the same language, there’s a wide range of cultural differences between life in the UK and the USA.

‌



Though the countries may seem quite similar, people who are brave enough to move from one to the other soon notice the many contrasts between them. Lots of people document their experiences of moving abroad and living in a new country on social media.

‌



This is the case with Ashley Jackson, who originally comes from Austin, Texas, but moved to Stretford in Greater Manchester in April 2022 with her husband Andi, who comes from Preston in Lancashire. The couple share two children, Levon and Matilda.

‌



The mum, who posts content online as @themossycactus, recently took to TikTok and said that despite how much she “loves it here”, there are three British things she’s “super not into”.

The first is something everyone hates - potholes. These frustrating bowl-shaped dents found on many UK roads can make driving feel that bit more perilous. Ashley said: “They seem to be the norm around here… I just see them everywhere. It’s crazy.

“Riding my bike or when we’re driving in the car or walking to school, like, there’s so many potholes and they’ve all been patched up, too. Not all of them, there’s still potholes, but it’s like a patchwork quilt out here.”

‌



The next complaint Ashley had was about the “super long referral times” to see an NHS specialist. She continued: “The NHS needs help and I think we need to focus on that because it’s a really great system.”

But her third complaint is where things took a turn. Ashley went on: “Might be controversial, but Jaffa Cakes. Not my fave - they’re dry, orange, I’m not really into orange chocolatey stuff. It’s not my favourite biscuit that you guys do here - there’s loads better ones.”

In the comments section, many TikTok users shared her frustrations with potholes - though some Americans pointed out their prevalence in the US, too - as well as the lengthy wait times associated with the NHS. But Ashley’s disdain for Jaffa Cakes - and the fact she branded them a “biscuit” - caused a stir.

‌



The first Jaffa Cake was created almost 100 years ago, and they’ve remained a firm favourite staple in many supermarkets and stores across the nation, with most shops offering own brand versions too.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

Regardless of whether it’s the original McVitie’s Jaffa Cake or a generic version, they’re typically found in the biscuit aisle - despite being legally considered a cake after a 1991 VAT ruling.

Article continues below

One TikTok user commented: “I was with you until you said Jaffa Cakes, JAFFA CAKES. Nope, no. Too far.”

Another agreed: “You lost me at not liking Jaffa Cakes”. A third said: “Jaffa cakes went to court in 1991 in a tribunal to be officially designated a cake not a biscuit” while a fourth commented: “The clues in the name Jaffa CAKES! Not biscuits.”

Someone else said: “Agree with the first two……..but Jaffa cakes! No, they are fantastic.” Another joked: “Jaffa Cakes how dare you” while another advised: “Those of you in the US, you can get Jaffa cakes at Aldi.”

News.title: Golders Green terror attack suspect was 'known to police' before two stabbed in rampage
News.content:
Golders Green terror attack suspect was 'known to police' before two stabbed in rampage

The man accused of carrying out an antisemitic terror attack in Golders Green had reportedly been referred to the Government’s counter-extremism Prevent programme - this is a breaking story

View Image The suspect had reportedly been referred to the Government’s counter-extremism Prevent programme (Image: .)

The man suspected of stabbing two men in Golders Green is understood to have previously been referred to the Government’s counter-extremism Prevent programme.

The 45-year-old suspect had been referred to the multi-agency programme that places a legal duty on public bodies to identify people who may turn to extremism, the BBC reported on Thursday.

Counter-terror officers working on the programme collaborate with local authority partners and community organisations to help identify and support vulnerable people. If a person is assessed as being at risk of terrorism, they may be referred to Home Office’s Channel Programme.

Two Jewish men - named locally as 34-year-old Shloime Rand and 76-year-old Moshe Shine - were taken to hospital after being stabbed in north London late on Wednesday morning in an attack police are treating as a terrorist incident. The suspect, said by police to be a British national born in Somalia, was arrested following the incident. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said the man came to the UK “lawfully as a child” in the 1990s.

Speaking at a roundtable on Thursday, Sir Keir Starmer said the criminal justice response to the attack must be "swift, agile and visible" shortly after extra funding was announced to increase security for Jewish communities.

Article continues below

A further £25 million will be invested to boost police patrols and protections around synagogues, schools and community centres, taking the total commitment this year to £58 million. Legislation creating proscription-like powers to pursue people and organisations acting on behalf of malign state-sponsored groups will also be "fast-tracked" in the coming weeks, ministers saId.

News.title: Amateur firebreather set fire to own face when stunt went wrong
News.content:
Amateur firebreather set fire to own face when stunt went wrong

Joe, from Somerset, is self-taught

Horrifying moment firebreather set fire to own face when stunt went wrong

This is the horrifying moment a fire-breather's head went up in flames when a stunt went wrong - causing his face to 'melt' off. Joe Johnstone performed the stunt at a barbecue in Bridgwater, Somerset, on April 7 when a gust of wind caused his beard to catch on fire.

‌



The 31-year-old said he hadn't performed for two years until being asked to by kids at the gathering, prompting him to show them his tricks. Shocking footage shows Joe spinning a lit fire staff before fire breathing, blowing a liquid fuel onto the flame to create a stream of fire, before it blows back into his face, setting his beard alight.

‌



Seconds later, Joe's entire head is ablaze and he drops to the ground clutching his face as concerned pals rush over to help. The self-taught fire-breather said they managed to pat out the flames before putting him under a cold shower until an ambulance arrived.

‌



View 5 Images Joe went up in flames (Kennedy News and Media)

The thrill seeker was rushed to Southmead Hospital in Bristol where he said doctors had to 'peel off' the melted, dead skin from his face. Joe, who doesn't work, described it as the 'worst pain' he'd ever experienced and that it had to be done every four hours.

The self-professed 'fire warrior' was discharged after seven days in hospital and, despite the accident, is looking forward to going back to fire-breathing. Joe, from Bridgwater, Somerset, said: "I've done it a million times. We were having a barbeque and the kids were like, 'can you show us?'

‌



"I said 'I haven't done it in a couple of years, I'm a bit rusty.' A gust of wind just came and blew it back in my face, simple as that. In these situations, you just have to be calm. I put my hands in my face trying to save what I could save, trying to keep it out of my eyes.

View 5 Images Joe taught himself the trick (Kennedy News and Media)

"It was the most frightening time of my life. It wasn't that windy but sometimes a gust of wind comes out of nowhere. It was quite a dry day as well. I didn't feel my face on fire, my brain just went on survival mode.

‌



"I wasn't really thinking about the pain, all I was thinking was 'how can I put this out?'. That was the only thing going through my head. My friends started hitting the fire and they dragged me to the shower, I had cold water all over my face. I was in the shower for half an hour until the ambulance came.

View 5 Images Joe's whole head was on fire (Kennedy News and Media)

"The pain came after I was put out. The most painful thing was in the hospital when the doctors came in and they said they have to take the dead skin off my face.

‌



"They scrubbed my face and it was the worst hour of my life. My face is definitely melted. It didn't look like me, it didn't look normal."

View 5 Images Joe was taken to the hospital with serious burns (Kennedy News and Media)

Joe started fire-breathing eight years ago after seeing people perform in festivals and is self-taught and grateful to have survived the accident. Joe said: "I started going to festivals about eight years ago. I'd seen people do it in underground raves and I fancied doing it myself.

‌



"I saw people do it and thought I wanted to do that. I just picked it up and started doing it myself. I've been to a few festivals in the last few years. I can taste, smell, talk, see, the fact that I'm still alive is a miracle. I'm so lucky."

Joe posted a 10-second clip of his accident on social media to raise awareness and said he enjoys 'staring death in the face'. Joe said: "I put the video up for other people's awareness. I couldn't believe how big the flames were on my face, it was intense watching it. I can't wait to get back to it."

View 5 Images Joe says he will be more careful next time (Kennedy News and Media)

Article continues below

"Nothing is going to scare me. The reason it happened was because I put it down for a couple of years. I used to be really good. I have to make sure there is a bucket next to me, I'll wet my face, check the wind. I like staring death in the face, I do like pushing myself, I'm a fire warrior."

News.title: Reduce the risk of high blood pressure by cutting one food group
News.content:
Reduce the risk of high blood pressure by cutting one food group

High blood pressure is a serious health problem that can lead to life-threatening illnesses like heart attacks and strokes, but it presents very few early symptoms and you may have it without knowing

View 2 Images High blood pressure actually presents very few early symptoms (Image: Westend61 via Getty Images)

High blood pressure is a serious health problem that can lead to life-threatening illnesses like heart attacks and strokes. It can also increase your risk of serious conditions like kidney disease and vascular dementia.

‌



But despite how potentially devastating it is, high blood pressure actually presents very few early symptoms, and you may well have it without knowing. So it's very important to do what you can to minimise your risk of developing high blood pressure, which is also known as hypertension.

‌



There are some risk factors you can't really do anything about because they involve your age, ethnicity and family history. But there are some that are definitely within your control.

‌



What is high blood pressure?

High blood pressure is when the force of blood pushing against the walls of your blood vessels is too high. If blood pressure stays high for too long, it can damage the walls of blood vessels, causing tears.

To fix these, the body sends special cells that stick to the site, explains the American Heart Association. Over time, substances, such as cholesterol and fats may also build up at these damaged spots.

As these build up, the inside of the arteries become narrower and this blocks the flow of blood (and causes the heart to work harder), further increasing blood pressure and potentially causing heart failure, heart attack, stroke and even kidney failure, reports Surrey Live.

‌



View 2 Images Avoid salty food which can help lower your blood pressure (Image: Synergee via Getty Images)

Symptoms of high blood pressure

High blood pressure does not usually cause any symptoms, so many people have it without realising it. In fact, the only way to find out for sure if you have high blood pressure is to get your blood pressure checked, usually at your doctor's surgery or at a pharmacy, when a cuff is usually wrapped around your upper arm and filled with air until it feels tight.

However, high blood pressure can on rare occasions cause symptoms which might be noticeable. They include:

‌



Headaches

Vision changes

Chest pain

Shortness of breath

Dizziness or vertigo

Nosebleeds

Fatigue or confusion

Heart palpitations

Facial flushing or blood spots in eyes

What causes high blood pressure?

There are many different things that can cause high blood pressure. These are the main ones:

your age — you are more likely to get high blood pressure the older you get)

having close relatives with high blood pressure

your ethnicity — you're at higher risk if you have a Black African, Black Caribbean or South Asian ethnic background

smoking

drinking alcohol

being overweight

feeling stressed over a long period

an unhealthy diet

‌



How you can help lower blood pressure

You can be prescribed medicine for high blood pressure by a doctor. Healthy lifestyle changes can also help lower your blood pressure, says the NHS. Key things you can do are:

Have a healthy, balanced diet that includes plenty of fruits, vegetables and whole grains

Do not eat too much salt - avoid salty food (lots of ultra-processed food is high in salt) or adding too much salt to your meals

Exercise regularly – aim to do at least 150 minutes of exercise a week

Lose weight if you're overweight

Don't drink too much alcohol – avoid drinking more than 14 alcohol units a week on a regular basis

Don't drink too much caffeine

Don't smoke

One diet in particular can help prevent or alleviate high blood pressure. The DASH diet stands for Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension and was specifically designed with blood pressure in mind. It encourages an increased intake of fibre and essential minerals like calcium, potassium, and magnesium. At the same time, it aims to reduce sodium and unhealthy fats in one's diet. It has been called the world's "second healthiest diet".

‌



Which foods are bad for blood pressure?

You will be able to find lots of lists of foods that are bad for your blood pressure. But the one type of food that most experts list first is: salty foods. Most of the salt we eat comes already in our food, says the British Heart Foundation, even in things we don't think of as salty, like breakfast cereals. Ultra-processed foods, like salty snacks and supermarket-ready pizzas, are also high in salt. Another food high in salt is processed meat, which is known to be cancer-causing.

Other foods that can be bad for blood pressure are sugary and fatty foods. They do not, in fact, directly affect blood pressure but these are generally high-calorie foods - eating too much of them can lead to weight gain, which is linked to raised blood pressure.

Alcohol is also bad for blood pressure and, for some people, so is excess caffeine. A moderate intake of 4-5 cups of coffee a day should not be a problem for most people, says the BHF, but some people are more sensitive to caffeine than others and drinking too much caffeine may affect blood pressure.

‌



Here's a more detailed list of foods that can be bad for your blood pressure:

salty foods (like pizza, burgers, processed meats

sugary foods (like pre-made processed desserts, granola bars, cereals, fizzy drinks, fruit juices and energy drinks)

red meat (like beef, lamb and venison)

alcohol (this includes all alchol)

saturated fats (like pre-made desserts, processed meats like sausages and bacon, cooking fats like butter)

ultra-processed foods

What is processed meat?

The World Health Organisation says processed meat refers to "meat that has been transformed through salting, curing, fermentation, smoking, or other processes to enhance flavour or improve preservation".

News.title: Apocalyptic scenario if UK's power went down tomorrow as energy expert issues warning
News.content:
Apocalyptic scenario if UK's power went down tomorrow as energy expert issues warning

A senior energy expert has warned that a National Grid blackout could trigger widespread disruption across the UK, potentially mirroring the Spain and Portugal power outages

View 3 Images An expert has warned about what would happen if the UK suddenly lost power (Image: DARREN STAPLES, AFP via Getty Images)

In recent years, speculation has mounted over the resilience of the UK’s energy network, even as a growing proportion of electricity is generated from renewable sources. Much of this concern has been driven by escalating global tensions, raising questions about whether the system could withstand malicious attacks or weather events.

‌



Against this backdrop, a co-director of the UK Energy Research Centre has warned that, in the event of a major power outage, the situation could mirror blackouts seen in Spain and Portugal in recent years, with people becoming trapped in lifts and trains coming to a standstill.

‌



Those outages occurred when electricity supplies across the Iberian Peninsula abruptly failed, causing widespread disruption and prompting concerns about how a similar scenario might unfold in the UK.

‌



View 3 Images Professor Bell warned some trains would stop (Image: Getty)

Professor Bell told the i: “It would be quite similar to how things looked in Spain and Portugal. You'd get stuck in lifts, wherever they are in the lift shaft. Trains would get stopped - you might be in a diesel train but the signalling depends on electricity.

“In 2003 there was a localised power issue which affected only parts of London, but it was a hot August day and people were stuck in sweltering [underground] tunnels with no air conditioning.”

‌



Beyond transport disruption, Professor Bell warned that everyday essentials would also be affected, with fridges failing to preserve food and communication systems becoming unreliable.

He said: “Refrigerators will stop working, so you're worried about food going off....Your Wi-Fi stops working, too.

“Communication becomes difficult, because if you've got a battery on your phone, you can still try and find out what's going on, but you're dependent on the mobile phone networks staying up and running.”

‌



View 3 Images Last year there was a major power outage in Spain and Portugal (Image: Getty)

Professor Bell’s remarks come as millions of households grapple with high energy bills linked to the ongoing crisis in the Middle East.

They also follow comments from energy minister Michael Shanks, who argued that renewable energy could strengthen the UK’s national security by making the system less vulnerable to attack.

‌



Mr Shanks said this was because solar panels and wind farms are harder to target than fossil fuel power plants.

Speaking from Ukraine, which has endured repeated strikes by Russia strikes on its energy infrastructure, he told the Guardian: “Building a decentralised power system with a whole series of assets is less of a risk of physical attack than large-scale power stations.

“Moving towards clean power is the best way to deliver our energy security in an increasingly uncertain world....They [Ukraine] are building decarbonised infrastructure across the country because solar and wind and batteries are much harder to target than large scale power stations.”

Article continues below

Mr Shanks added that the UK could draw valuable lessons from Ukraine, not only on improving resilience to attacks but also on strengthening overall energy security.

News.title: Dates as sun to set after 9pm in UK for first time since 2025
News.content:
Dates as sun to set after 9pm in UK for first time since 2025

Lighter and hopefully warmer nights will soon be here

View Image The days have been getting longer for months (Image: Gary Yeowell/Getty)

The days have been gradually getting longer since the winter solstice back in December, with more and more daylight experienced across the UK. The clocks changing back in March have also led to later sunsets, and the UK is about to experience daylight after 9pm for the first time since 2025.

‌



Today, Thursday, April 30, this will be the case for the westernmost parts of the UK, including County Fermanagh in Northern Ireland. For London, though, it'll take roughly another 26 days, until May 26, before there's an after-9pm sunset. In Edinburgh the first post-9pm sunset is expected around May 6, and it's May 18 for Cardiff, and May 3 for Belfast, according to predictions.

‌



Sunset times will then become later and later until the summer solstice - the 'longest day of the year' - which in 2026 falls on Sunday, June 21. On this date the sun is forecast to set at 9.21pm in London, 10.02pm in Edinburgh, 9.33pm in Cardiff, and 10.04pm in Belfast.

Article continues below

After this, the sun’s position remains in pretty much the same place for a few days, before the days gradually shorten once more. During the solstice, according to English Heritage, the earth’s axis is tilted at its closest point from the sun, meaning that in the northern hemisphere, the sun is at its highest point in the sky.

The summer solstice is often celebrated by many different countries and cultures around the world.

News.title: Golders Green terror attack latest: Suspect ‘known to government’s counter-extremism programme before stabbing’
News.content:
Golders Green Stabbing- Starmer Says Suspected Terror Attack Must Receive ‘Swift And Agile’ Response

Sir Keir Starmer urged the criminal justice system must respond in a “swift, agile, and visible way” to a suspected terrorist attack in Golders Green after an adviser said the Jewish community is at “breaking point”.

Speaking on Thursday, the prime minister said there was “no getting away” from the fact the victims were targeted because they are Jewish.

Government adviser on antisemitism Lord John Mann said the UK’s Jewish community is at “breaking point” in the wake of the double stabbing.

Attack victim Shilome Rand, 34, also accused the government of "not doing its job" in protecting the Jewish community.

The Metropolitan Police force confirmed that the 45-year-old suspect, who was arrested at the scene on suspicion of attempted murder, is a British national who was born in Somalia. Police said the suspect had a “history of serious violence and mental health issues”.

On Thursday morning the government said an additional £25 million will be invested to increase police patrols and security to keep Jewish communities safe. It added legislation will be fast-tracked in the coming weeks to target those acting on behalf of state-sponsored groups.

Zack Polanski has accused Labour of “using Jewish pain” to justify an “authoritarian” agenda in considering banning pro-Palestinian marches after the Golders Green attack.

The Green Party leader, who is the only current Jewish leader of a major political party in the UK, hit out at home secretary Shabana Mahmood as she hinted at using new powers for a crackdown on marches protesting against Israel.

The row broke out as the Jewish community reels from an antisemitic terror attack in Golders Green, the centre of London’s Jewish community, on Wednesday. During the attack, a 45-year-old man stabbed two Jewish men – one in his seventies and the other in his thirties – before being brought down by local police.

There are growing calls for tougher action against antisemitism, including from Chief Rabbi Sir Ephraim Mirvis, in the wake of the attack

Some have called for a suspension of pro-Palestine marches in the wake of an attack. Earlier, Ms Mahmood had hinted that a new law brought in by Labour could be used to stop marches from going ahead after Jonathan Hall, the terror laws watchdog, said antisemitic language is “incubated” in the protests.

But Mr Polanski told The Independent: “It is an outrage that this increasingly authoritarian government would now seek to use the pain of the Jewish community to seek further restrictions on the rights to peaceful protest. The Green Party will fight any restrictions on peaceful protest, whatever the cause, every step of the way.”

The Gaza issue has become a major dividing line between Labour and the Greens, with Mr Polanski’s party recently winning the Gorton and Denton by-election in Manchester, where part of its strategy was to target Muslim voters.

According to polling expert Lord Robert Hayward, Labour are set to lose 1,850 of their council seats in the 7 May local elections while the Greens are expected to gain 500.

open image in gallery Zack Polanski: ‘For other politicians to use antisemitism as a political football ... is utterly appalling and should be beneath them’ ( PA )

The Green Party is particularly projected to replace Labour in large parts of London, with all 32 borough councils up for election.

Labour’s balanced approach to Gaza and refusal to ban weapons sales to Israel has been one of the factors that has led to supporters and former members switching to the Greens.

Mr Polanski went on: “Jewish communities are waking up this morning feeling incredibly scared after another attack in this wave of odious antisemitic attacks.

“This is a time for politicians to work together to protect Jewish people – but some party leaders are instead using this moment to make party political attacks.”

He added: “I am the only Jewish leader of a major political party and I suffer antisemitic abuse every single day. For other politicians to use antisemitism as a political football, especially after these horrific attacks, is utterly appalling and should be beneath them.

“We must also be very clear that any response to these abhorrent attacks that curtails our civil liberties would be wrong. For a government to seek to use the pain of the Jewish community to restrict our right to peaceful protest would be a dangerous error.

open image in gallery Shabana Mahmood has hinted at banning pro-Palestine marches ( Getty )

“We must not respond to grave moments like this by turning inwards, or by clamping down on our hard-won rights. Instead, we must stand firm both in defending communities against such attacks and by confidently protecting the right of all of us to peaceful protest.”

Asked by BBC Radio 4’s Today Programme whether she thinks that sometimes pro-Palestine marches can foster hate towards British jews, Ms Mahmood said: “Yes. I mean, look, it’s certainly the case that, of course, the right to protest is a fundamental British freedom, and people from across the political spectrum use that freedom in order to make their point.

“That is how we work as a democracy, and it’s an important freedom that we, all of us, have.

“But certainly there are far too many instances at protests where crimes are committed, where hate crime is committed. And also the scale of those protests, the intensity, the repeat nature of protests has placed particular pressures on the Jewish community, especially, but not limited, limited to in London."

Earlier, she told BBC Breakfast: “I have already changed the law, and I won’t hesitate to do so again.”

The Bank of England (BoE) has voted to hold interest rates at 3.75 per cent, as they balance up the perils of rising inflation with an underperforming economic background.

With the Iran war again pushing up the price of oil this week, higher energy bills and rising costs across food and manufacturing are likely for much of 2026, putting additional pressure on households and businesses.

The Bank’s Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) cautioned that the conflict in the Middle East leaves global energy costs “highly uncertain” and that inflation is “likely to be higher” as the year progresses. Members voted 8-1 in favour of holding rates as a result, with one vote for an immediate hike in rates, highlighting the potential for rises to come over summer.

Interest rates were on a downward path after being cut four times last year, with early expectation being that another two cuts could follow in 2026 as inflation headed back towards the 2 per cent target.

However, the Iran war has changed all that and some experts argue that rates will need to be lifted again to combat the incoming inflation rise, the start of which was already evident in March’s UK economic figures, shifting up to 3.3 per cent.

Reacting to rates being held, chancellor Rachel Reeves said: “The war in the Middle East is not our war, but it is one we have to respond to. Every choice I make will be about keeping costs down for families and businesses, without repeating the mistakes we’ve seen in the past that resulted in higher inflation and higher interest rates.

“We entered this conflict in a stronger position because of the choices this government took to build economic stability, and we are going further to take back our energy security, backing British industry and protecting households, to build a Britain that is stronger, more resilient, and prepared for the future.”

In mid-March, the MPC voted 9-0 to maintain the bank rate at 3.75 per cent as it waited to see both the duration and impact of the war, which was then only a couple of weeks in.

But six weeks later there is no sign of a resolution, the Strait of Hormuz remains effectively closed to the passage of oil tankers and domestically, businesses have already started to note the impact through either falling exports or needing to pass on price rises, with high street sales expected to continue lower and SMEs seeing sales growth fall to a two-year low, according to the latest release of Xero’s Small Business Index.

The Bank of England’s analysis shows that households are expecting an inflationary hit this year and may already have reigned in spending with increased sensitivity to price changes.

And while a worst-case scenario of prolonged conflict could see inflation tip towards six per cent in the months following a war resolution, the BoE notes that a looser labour market can restrict the worst of inflationary pressures. The UK has had rising unemployment recently, hitting 5 per cent at the start of the year, meaning works could have less power to earn salary rises and firms then more readily have spare capacity to absorb some cost increases.

The Bank are, noted governor Andrew Bailey, monitoring the “impact on the UK economy very closely”.

Interest rates are at 3.75% ( Bank of England )

Sir Mel Stride MP, shadow chancellor, said: “Rachel Reeves has weakened our economy and left us vulnerable in the run up to the latest energy crisis. The conflict in the Middle East is pushing up prices - but the UK already had the highest inflation in the G7 thanks to Labour’s choices.

“Tax hikes, reckless spending and disastrous energy policies have paved the way for high inflation and interest rates staying higher for longer. We need a different approach: cutting the benefits bill, lowering taxes and drilling in the North Sea. We need to Get Britain Working Again.”

Several research groups have negated any potential benefit of additional North Sea drilling to energy prices in the UK, both in terms of lowering the benchmark cost of oil and as a long-term solution to rising costs.

One of the UK’s leading think tanks has called on the government to cap energy costs for the short term, while also pushing for a renewed focus on green energy.

“While the Bank held rates constant, they have clearly stated that the situation could get worse before it gets better. If energy markets do not improve very quickly, they will likely raise rates and keep them higher for longer - hitting growth and hurting households,” said Carsten Jung, associate director at the IPPR.

“The government is not powerless in this. Temporarily capping energy costs can limit inflation increases and can be cheaper than being hit by big second round effects and having to clean up a recession later.

“As these shocks become more frequent in a more volatile world, reducing our reliance on fossil fuels is the smart move to protect the economy moving forward.”

Elsewhere, some mortgage lenders have reduced rates over the past week or two, as swap rates fell back slightly following sharp rises in the early weeks of the war, which led to the best deals being pulled.

However, even with the BoE interest rate held, it remains unlikely that a huge range of low-cost mortgages will be on the comeback soon. Markets are still pricing in up to three interest rate hikes and, even if that number does not materialise in BoE terms, high street banks still price their products off those figures.

For savers, however, it should be good news, with several financial institutions still offering good rates well above 4 per cent - and one expert thinks they could yet go higher.

“To keep the value of your savings intact, it pays to shop around. The good news is that there are lots of inflation-beating options available,” said Finder’s Kate Steere, personal finance expert.

“I’d urge savers to avoid tying themselves into a fixed deal at the moment. Instead, check out the top easy access options and set a reminder to review your accounts in a few months, when any upward movement in the base rate may well be reflected in even more competitive savings rates.”

The National Debtline service say they are seeing initial signs of concern among callers which indicate cost of living worries.

“A hold in interest rates won’t bring immediate relief to many households,” said head of debt advice communications, Grace Brownfield. “While we haven’t yet seen a rise in mortgage arrears among people contacting National Debtline, we are seeing more people struggling with everyday costs, particularly energy bills and credit cards.

“These are often the first warning signs of wider financial difficulty, especially for households already under pressure from higher prices and stagnant incomes.”

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth delivered a defiant and aggressive testimony on Wednesday before the House Armed Services Committee.

While the testimony was billed as being about the Pentagon’s budget, it inevitably became about the War in Iran. During the testimony, Hegseth was sometimes outright belligerent. My colleague Holly Baxter said that he sounded increasingly deluded and desperate, hoping to win the support of the audience of one that is Donald Trump.

At one point, he gallingly said that “the biggest adversary we face at this point are the reckless, feckless and defeatist words of congressional Democrats and some Republicans.”

A few days ago, I hid under a table during the White House Correspondents’ Dinner as I saw Hegseth bolt out of the Washington Hilton after a shooter allegedly came to try and take out Trump. But here, he showed absolutely zero signs of trying to turn down the tone in the country.

“Choosing to call out Democrats and some Republicans as our greatest threat, amidst all the threats, including an act of war, shows you what a f***ng joke he is,” Rep. Pat Ryan of New York, a West Point graduate, told The Independent. “I asked them questions about six Americans that were killed, and he wouldn't even answer in a straightforward way.”

open image in gallery U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth departs after testifying before the House Armed Services Committee April 29, 2026 ( Getty )

Even Rep. Jen Kiggans (R-Va.), who represents the Navy-heavy Virginia Beach, grilled Hegseth about the dismissal of the Secretary of the Navy John Phelan.

But if Hegseth had a rough go at it at the House of Representatives, he will have an even tougher time before the Senate Armed Services Committee on Thursday.

There, he will have to face Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.), whom he has tried to punish for a video he put out with Democratic lawmakers saying U.S. servicemembers have a right to refuse illegal orders.

Members who are not on the committee will also be watching Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), who voted to confirm Hegseth, but has at times become more critical of the Trump administration while avoiding directly criticizing the president.

“I think that we need details,” Tillis told The Independent. We need to know what the strategic objectives are. What does success look like? What is the build-up for the budget request?”

And this is to say nothing of the Republicans who voted against his confirmation: Sens. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Susan Collins of Maine and Mitch McConnell of Kentucky. McConnell especially criticized the Pentagon.

This week, the usually taciturn McConnell put out an op-ed in The Washington Post criticizing the fact that the Pentagon has not spent $400 billion that the Senate set aside for Ukraine.

open image in gallery Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-KY) hit out at the Pentagon for not spending money meant for Ukraine ( Getty )

“Trump’s focus on ending the war is noble,” he said. “But the price and stability of peace matter. The Pentagon’s approach of withholding or slow-rolling support to Ukraine is in effect the same strategy President Joe Biden deployed.”

For someone like McConnell, the chairman of the Appropriations Committee’s subcommittee on military spending, this was a damning condemnation. McConnell did not mention Hegset,h but it was a clear message for him to get it together.

The Senate as a whole is more hawkish than the House, so Hegseth might not face as much criticism about the war in Iran itself as about his management of the war. And the Senate does not take kindly to people dictating what it cannot know.

A common trait of the Trump White House has been members of the administration avoiding accountability or congressional oversight and then immediately melting in front of a committee.

Homeland Security Kristi Noem avoided the Senate Judiciary Committee for months, only for Tillis and Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) to eviscerate her. A few days later, she was gone. In February, Attorney General Pam Bondi faced a round of tough questioning about files related to Jeffrey Epstein, giving an equally pugnacious performance. By April, she got the boot.

This isn’t to say that Hegseth will suffer the same fate as the ladies. But as more members lose patience with him and as Republicans want to find someone to blame other than Trump, he might be the next sacrificial lamb.

News.title: British white supremacist found guilty of plotting gun attack after MI5 sting
News.content:
